title: Sell Mineral Rights in Illinois
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Illinois | Basin Interests
metaDescription: Small, steady Illinois basin oil check from Wabash, White, or Marion County? We read waterflood statements every week and buy legacy interests outright.
heroLead: Illinois basin checks are usually small, usually steady, and usually come from a waterflood unit that has been quietly producing for longer than most people realize.
intro: Southeastern Illinois, Wabash, White, Lawrence, and the fields around Salem in Marion County, has been producing oil since before the First World War, and a huge share of what is still on production today runs through waterflood, injecting water into depleted reservoirs to push remaining oil toward the producing wells. It is unglamorous, low-volume work, and that is exactly why it has lasted this long.

If you hold an Illinois basin interest, you are likely looking at a small monthly check that has been remarkably consistent for years, sometimes decades. That consistency is the whole story here, and it is also what makes these interests genuinely valuable to price correctly rather than dismiss because the gross numbers look modest.

sections.heading: Small Checks Are Not the Same as Worthless Checks
paragraphs: A $40 or $60 monthly check from a waterflood unit can look unimpressive next to what people hear about shale wells in Texas, but a steady $40 check that has held roughly flat for fifteen years is a very different asset than a $400 check on a well six months into a shale decline curve. Predictability has real value, and it is often underpriced by owners who assume small means unimportant.

We look at your full payment history when we can get it, rather than only the most recent statement, because a long, flat trend line is exactly the kind of data that lets us make a confident offer on a small legacy interest. That history is genuinely more useful to us than any single month's number, so it is worth digging out old statements if you have kept them.

sections.heading: Reading a Waterflood Statement
paragraphs: Waterflood operating costs show up differently than a standard producing well because water handling and injection are ongoing expenses baked into the field's economics. If your statement shows a line for water disposal or injection costs, that is normal for this kind of secondary recovery and does not mean the well is struggling.

What matters more is the trend over several months. A waterflood unit that has held a stable volume for years is generally close to its natural sustained rate, and that stable rate is the anchor point we use when calculating an offer.

sections.heading: Ownership Here Is Often Multi-Generational
paragraphs: Illinois basin production has been running long enough that a lot of current owners are third or fourth generation, and interests have been split among heirs repeatedly since the original lease. It is common for an owner to hold a fraction of a fraction, sometimes well under one percent of a unit.

That does not stop a sale from happening. We just need the division order or a recent statement showing your specific decimal interest so the offer reflects exactly what you own, not what the whole unit produces.

sections.heading: Selling a Legacy Illinois Basin Interest
paragraphs: Because these fields decline so gradually, the case for selling usually comes down to what you would rather have: a small, steady check continuing indefinitely at roughly the same level, or a lump sum now that you can use for something with a clearer near-term purpose.

The process itself is simple. We confirm your interest against county records, most often in Wabash, White, Marion, or Clark County, prepare a mineral deed, and close typically within a few weeks once the paperwork is in order. Multi-generational ownership sometimes means a short delay while heirship documentation is gathered, but it rarely stops a sale from closing.

faqs.question: Your Illinois check is only $30 to $50 a month. Is it worth selling?
faqs.answer: Yes, in many cases. What matters is the stability of that number over time, not the size. A long, flat production history on a small check is exactly the kind of asset we can put a fair number on.

faqs.question: Why does your statement mention water injection costs?
faqs.answer: Most Illinois basin oil today is produced through waterflood, a secondary recovery method that injects water to push oil toward producing wells. The associated costs are a normal, ongoing part of that process, not a sign of a problem.

faqs.question: Can an owner sell a tiny fractional share of a unit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Illinois basin ownership is frequently split many ways after generations of inheritance, and offers are simply scaled to your exact decimal interest as shown on your division order or statement.

faqs.question: Are new wells being drilled in the Illinois basin?
faqs.answer: New drilling is limited today compared to the field's early-1900s buildout. Most current activity is maintaining and managing existing waterflood units rather than adding new wells.

faqs.question: What documents do you need to sell an inherited Illinois interest?
faqs.answer: A recent division order or statement showing your decimal interest is the main thing, along with anything establishing how the interest passed to you, a will, a prior deed, or probate paperwork if it went through an estate.

faqs.question: Could your Illinois basin well be revived with new drilling technology?
faqs.answer: It is possible in theory, but there is no widespread pattern of operators returning to old Illinois basin waterflood units with modern horizontal techniques. We price based on the well's actual current production rather than a hypothetical future workover.
